feedback: If a pupil limits the link to obvious tropical foods, read a soap or bread label together and surface the palm oil.
If a pupil thinks soy is mainly eaten by people as tofu, clarify that most soy worldwide feeds livestock, so it is hidden behind meat and eggs.
Praise concrete label-reading evidence rather than guessing: 'You found palm oil listed — that's the kind of clue to look for.'
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforest products are not only exotic jungle foods — many are hidden ingredients in ordinary goods, including palm oil, soy animal feed, rubber and timber.
learnerActions: Read real ingredient labels on everyday packaging together (biscuits, bread, soap, shampoo), and check product descriptions or material labels for items like trainers, which do not carry ingredient lists.

List the non-obvious rainforest-linked ingredients — palm oil or palm derivatives in some soaps and breads, natural rubber in some trainer soles (many use synthetic rubber), and soy animal feed behind much meat and many eggs (not shown on the label).
Sort products into 'obvious tropical treat' (chocolate, bananas, coffee) versus 'hidden ingredient' and discuss why the hidden ones are easy to miss.
Spot certification labels where they appear (Rainforest Alliance frog, FSC, RSPO) and discuss what signal they send.
activities.title: Hidden ingredients hunt

feedback: If sequencing is wrong, ask what has to happen to raw forest produce before it can reach a shelf (it must be grown, processed, shipped, manufactured).
For the certified question, if a pupil picks 'boycott', remind them a boycott removes smallholder income and the incentive to farm sustainably.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the chain order, the product→ingredient links, and the reasoning that certified sourcing is usually better than both careless buying and a blanket boycott.
learnerActions: Order the stages of the palm-oil journey in sequence: forest → plantation → processing/refinery → shipping → factory → shelf → home.
Match everyday products to their hidden rainforest ingredient (biscuit→palm oil, tyre→rubber, chicken nugget→soy feed, furniture→timber).
Answer: how does choosing a certified product help a forest compared with buying carelessly OR boycotting everything?
activities.title: Sequence and match the journey (check and consolidate)

feedback: If a pupil says distant shopping has no effect, trace one concrete product (palm oil in biscuits, or soy fed to nugget chicken) back to the land where it was grown, which in some supply chains is cleared forest, to show how demand pulls supply.
If a pupil insists boycott is ideal, explain palm oil is the highest-yielding oil crop so alternatives can need MORE land, and that certification rewards good practice a boycott cannot.
Reward answers that get BOTH halves and apply them to a fresh product, not slogans like 'rainforest products are bad'.
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine supply-chain reasoning holds both halves: everyday shopping IS connected through demand, AND a blanket boycott is not the best answer because it harms smallholders and removes the reward for farming sustainably.
learnerActions: Respond to a friend's claim: 'My shopping in Britain can't possibly affect a rainforest thousands of miles away — and anyway, the best thing to do is boycott every single rainforest product.'
State clearly whether the friend is right on EACH of the two points, and explain WHY for each half.
Apply the reasoning to a NEW product of the pupil's choice: pick something used this morning and trace an ingredient back toward a rainforest, saying where to look on the label.
Discuss trade-offs: if everyone boycotted palm oil tomorrow, who is helped and who harmed; and is it fair to expect a family on a tight budget to pay more for certified goods?
activities.title: Argue the diagnostic both ways
